newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin blasted for Chechen deal, PM goes to Paris.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin blasted for Chechen deal, PM goes to Paris.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's communist opponents in parliament said on Monday they may try to impeach him for withdrawing all remaining Russian troops from Chechnya and for Moscow's accord with the region's separatists.

But with power concentrated in Yeltsin's hands under Russia's constitution the impeachment moves stand little chance of success and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin signalled business as usual by setting off on a planned visit to France.

The row between Yeltsin and his opponents erupted over the weekend after the Kremlin revealed new concessions to the Chechen rebels which were effectively a recognition of Moscow's utter military defeat after nearly two years of war.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, while insisting he wanted no resumption of hostilities, accused Yeltsin of treason and his Kremlin entourage of scheming behind parliament's back to break up Russia in the same way as the Soviet Union shattered in 1991.

The accord, signed on Saturday by Chernomyrdin and Chechen government leader Aslan Maskhadov, the man who led the guerrillas to victory over Moscow's regular troops, was a "malignant tumour", Zyuganov said on Sunday.

The communist chairman of parliament's security committee told reporters an emergency debate on the Chechen deal, called at communist insistence for next Friday, should discuss impeachment and a vote of no confidence in the government.

"The deputies are not going to limit themselves to generating hot air," Viktor Ilyukhin said of next Friday's debate in the lower house. "I think the questions of impeachment and of confidence in the government will be raised."

Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma, was more cautious, saying the lower house would consider over the next few days whether the accords breached the constitution, notably by giving in to Chechen demands for independence.
If there has been a constitutional fault, then the question of impeachment could be raised on Friday, Seleznyov said.

It is unlikely to get far, however. Impeachment requires two-thirds majorities in both chambers of parliament and the approval of both the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court -- all within a time limit of three months.
The Duma also has little power to oust Chernomyrdin and the government against Yeltsin's wishes.
Chernomyrdin flew to Paris late on Monday for two days of talks on bilateral economic relations.

At Moscow's Vnukovo airport Chernomyrdin told reporters Russia would honour debts run up by the tsarist government and later reneged on by Soviet communists, though he said details had still to be worked out.

Many of the heirs to the tsar's creditors live in France and are claiming back some 140 to 160 billion French francs (($27.5-$31 billion) taking account of unpaid interest since the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.

Asked if he intended to finalise an agreement to repay the debts while in France, he said: "We will. I think today we will resolve this question. We will, because we are Russia. We will pay all our debts."

The announcement followed Russia's debut last week on the international capital markets with a $1.0 billion five-year Eurobond. It was not placed in France because of the outstanding compensation claims by the holders of tsarist debt.

Earlier on Monday Chernomyrdin met Yeltsin at the sanatorium near Moscow where the president is convalescing from his November 5 heart operation. The two men discussed the weekend's Chechen deal during their 90-minute meeting. ($1=5.118 French Franc)
